questions.stem:
Statements: X = W > R = T < Q.
Conclusions: I. Q > R   II. Q ≥ X.
Which conclusions follow? “Either” means at least one must hold, although neither is individually guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Answer: Only I follows. Trace the chain, retaining strict and equal signs. I is definitely true; II is not guaranteed. The selected conclusion follows across every weak ordering consistent with the statements.

questions.stem:
Statements: P > X = V = W > R.
Conclusions: I. R ≥ P   II. P ≥ V.
Which conclusions follow? “Either” means at least one must hold, although neither is individually guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Answer: Only II follows. Trace the chain, retaining strict and equal signs. I is not guaranteed; II is definitely true. The selected conclusion follows across every weak ordering consistent with the statements.

questions.stem:
Statements: U < W > T < Q > S.
Conclusions: I. T < U   II. W > S.
Which conclusions follow? “Either” means at least one must hold, although neither is individually guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Answer: Neither I nor II follows. Trace the chain, retaining strict and equal signs. I is not guaranteed; II is not guaranteed. The selected conclusion follows across every weak ordering consistent with the statements.

questions.stem:
Statements: P < T = U < W > R.
Conclusions: I. W ≥ U   II. W < T.
Which conclusions follow? “Either” means at least one must hold, although neither is individually guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Answer: Only I follows. Trace the chain, retaining strict and equal signs. I is definitely true; II is not guaranteed. The selected conclusion follows across every weak ordering consistent with the statements.

questions.stem:
Statements: Only a few cards are branches. All branches are cheques. No cheques is a lockers.
Conclusions:
I. Some cards are not branches.
II. No branches is a lockers.
questions.explanation: Answer: Both I and II follow. Only a few means some are and some are not. All B are C and no C is D excludes every B from D.

questions.stem:
Statements: Only a few cards are branches. Some branches are cheques. All cheques are lockers.
Conclusions:
I. All cards are lockers.
II. No branches is a lockers.
questions.explanation: Answer: Neither I nor II follows. A need not be contained in D. Some B are C and therefore D, contradicting II.

questions.stem:
Statements: Some cards are branches. All branches are cheques. No cheques is a lockers.
Conclusions:
I. Some cards are cheques.
II. Some branches are lockers.
questions.explanation: Answer: Only I follows. The stated A–B overlap lies in C. Since B is contained in C, no B can be D.

questions.stem:
Statements: No cards is a branches. Some branches are cheques. All cheques are lockers.
Conclusions:
I. All cards are lockers.
II. Some lockers are branches.
questions.explanation: Answer: Only II follows. The B–C overlap is inside D, proving II. No universal A–D relation is given.

questions.stem: A surveyor walks 142 km north, turns right and walks 255 km, then turns right and walks 6 km. What is the shortest distance (km) from the starting point?
questions.explanation: Answer: 289. The first and third legs oppose each other. Net components are 136 km along the initial direction and 255 km perpendicular to it. Distance = √(136² + 255²) = 289 km.

questions.stem: A surveyor walks 34 km north, turns left and walks 60 km, then turns left and walks 2 km. What is the shortest distance (km) from the starting point?
questions.explanation: Answer: 68. The first and third legs oppose each other. Net components are 32 km along the initial direction and 60 km perpendicular to it. Distance = √(32² + 60²) = 68 km.

questions.stem: E is the brother of C. C is the mother of H. A is the father of E and C. How is E related to H?
questions.explanation: Answer: Maternal uncle. E is the brother of H’s mother C. Therefore E is the maternal uncle.

questions.stem: C is the mother of G. F is the son of G. D is the father of G. How is F related to D?
questions.explanation: Answer: Grandson. D is a parent of G, and F is G’s son. Hence F is D’s grandchild.

questions.stem: D is the only daughter of E. E is the father of D. H is the son of D. A is the sister of E. How is E related to H?
questions.explanation: Answer: Maternal grandfather. E is the father of D, and D is H’s mother. Thus E is the maternal grandfather.

questions.stem: In a queue of 45 candidates, a candidate is 15th from the front. After moving 3 places towards the back, what is the candidate’s rank from the back?
questions.explanation: Answer: 28. New front rank = 15+3 = 18. Back rank = 45 − 18 + 1 = 28.

questions.stem: In a queue of 48 candidates, a candidate is 12th from the front. After moving 4 places towards the back, what is the candidate’s rank from the back?
questions.explanation: Answer: 33. New front rank = 12+4 = 16. Back rank = 48 − 16 + 1 = 33.

Derived data: A: first category 360, second category 240; B: first category 960, second category 640; C: first category 1440, second category 1080; D: first category 760, second category 1140; E: first category 540, second category 360. Percentage difference = |total(A)+total(D)−total(C)| ÷ total(C) × 100.

questions.stem: A vessel contains 50 litres of milk and water in ratio 3:2. How many litres of pure milk must be added to make the ratio 2:1?
questions.explanation: Answer: 10. Milk = 3V/5, water = 2V/5. Solve (3V/5 + x)/(2V/5) = 2; x = V/5 = 10.

questions.stem: A village has 4100 registered customers. This increases by 20% in year 1 and decreases by 20% in year 2. What is the final number?
questions.explanation: Answer: 3936. Apply successive factors: 4100 × 120/100 × 80/100.

questions.stem: [Bar set] A new branch F has a total equal to the average total at A and E. Its categories are split in ratio 2:3. What is the number in its second category?
questions.explanation: Answer: 468. Derived data: A: first category 240, second category 360; B: first category 420, second category 560; C: first category 780, second category 1040; D: first category 1360, second category 1020; E: first category 600, second category 360. Average total = (total A + total E)/2. The second category is 3/5 of that average.

questions.stem: [Bar set] The business category at D is what percentage of the agricultural category at B? (Round to two decimal places.)

questions.stem: A train of length 140 m crosses a 120 m platform at 46.8 km/h. Find crossing time in seconds (to two decimals).
An item costs ₹1000. It is marked above cost and sold at a 10% discount on marked price, earning 20% profit. Find the marked price (₹, to two decimals).
questions.explanation: Answer: 1333.33. Selling price = 1000 × 120/100. Marked price = selling price ÷ 0.9 = 1333.33.

questions.stem: A can finish a job in 32 days and B in 48 days. They work together for 4 days, then B leaves. How many more days does A need? (Round to two decimal places if needed.)
questions.explanation: Answer: 25.33. Use 96 work units. Rates: A = 3, B = 2 units/day. Remaining = 96 − 4×5. Divide by A’s rate 3.

questions.stem: The average of 31 numbers is 47. One number, 59, is replaced and the average rises by 5. What is the new number?
questions.explanation: Answer: 214. Total increases by 31 × 5. New number = 59 + 155.
